notes: Dublin return certification challenge; Razgar Article 8 health consequences and wife's suicide risk analysed in detail.

enrichment.short_title: Ali v SSHD: Dublin certification and Article 8 health consequences of removal
key_facts: An Iranian asylum seeker arrived in the UK after claiming asylum in Germany under the Dublin Regulations and was certified under section 93(2)(b) as clearly unfounded on Article 8 grounds.
His wife and children claimed asylum in the UK; after his detention for removal she took a paracetamol overdose said to be linked to fear of his deportation.
Psychiatric evidence from Dr Steadman suggested a risk of further self-harm or suicide if the claimant were removed to Germany or the family returned to Iran.
An adjudicator had already rejected the wife's asylum and Article 8 appeals on credibility and medical grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's certification that the claimant's human rights claim was clearly unfounded.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Bennett J held the medical evidence did not meet the high Article 8 threshold and an adjudicator could not reasonably find a flagrant breach on removal to Germany.
enrichment.ratio: Article 8 may in principle be engaged by foreseeable health consequences of immigration removal even where Article 3 is not violated, but the threshold is high; on a section 93 certification the Secretary of State applies a screening test and may certify if, after careful review, the allegation must clearly fail.
legal_issues: Whether removal to Germany risked a flagrant breach of Article 8 through harm to the claimant's wife
The correct test for certification under section 93(2)(b)
Whether the wife's adjudicator determination bound assessment of the claimant's Article 8 claim
Weight to be given to Dr Steadman's uncritical reliance on the wife's account
linked_authorities: Razgar v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] UKHL 27
Mehmeti v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWHC 2999 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Statutory framework, medical evidence and dismissal are clearly reasoned though some adjudicator findings were not finally resolved.

notes: Bruton tenancy possession appeal; Kay applied to reject agent and encumbrance arguments.

enrichment.short_title: Islington v O'Shea: Patchwork licence termination and Bruton tenancy defences
key_facts: Islington licensed Patchwork Community Housing Association to use a house as temporary housing accommodation from 1987, terminable on 28 days' notice.
Patchwork granted occupiers including Gary O'Shea assured tenancies; Islington terminated Patchwork's licence in 2003 and sought possession.
O'Shea argued Patchwork acted as Islington's agent, or that Islington had consented to tenancies encumbering its freehold.
The county court and Court of Appeal held that termination of the head licence ended any derivative tenancy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from a county court possession order after Patchwork's licence was terminated.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; the Bruton tenant had no estate binding on Islington once Patchwork's licence ended.
enrichment.ratio: When a head licence or tenancy ends, any sub-tenancy derived from it automatically ends; a licence to provide temporary accommodation does not make the licensee the landlord's agent or authorise tenancies binding on the freeholder beyond the licence term.
legal_issues: Whether Patchwork had actual or ostensible authority to grant tenancies on Islington's behalf
Whether a Bruton tenancy could bind the licensor local authority
Whether Islington consented to encumbrances on its freehold
Application of Kay v Lambeth to short-life housing arrangements
linked_authorities: Bruton v London & Quadrant Housing Trust [2000] 1 AC 406
Kay v Lambeth London Borough Council [2004] EWCA Civ 926

confidence.notes: Core landlord and tenant propositions and dismissal are clearly and comprehensively reasoned.

notes: Michael Stone Chillenden appeal; Daley cell confession directions and fresh evidence grounds rejected.

enrichment.short_title: R v Stone: Chillenden murders appeal and prison informer directions
key_facts: Michael Stone was convicted after retrial of murdering Dr Lin Russell and Megan Russell and attempting to murder Josie Russell in Chillenden in 1996.
The prosecution case rested heavily on a cell confession alleged by fellow prisoner Damien Daley, a hardened criminal who admitted lying when it suited him.
Fresh psychiatric, drug abuse and misconduct material about Daley was received on appeal but held not to undermine the verdict.
Late evidence from Paul Gilheaney alleging Daley retracted his account was rejected as not capable of belief.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge on summing-up and fresh evidence grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge's directions to examine Daley's evidence with great care were adequate and no Pringle/Benedetto threshold warning was required on the facts.
enrichment.ratio: Cell confession cases require special attention but not fixed warnings in every case; where the confession contained detailed facts, defence counsel deliberately did not allege improper motive, and the jury knew the witness was deeply flawed, generic warnings about easy concoction or remand-prisoner advantage were unnecessary.
legal_issues: Whether the judge should have given a special bad-character and cell-confession warning
Admissibility and weight of fresh evidence about Daley's drug addiction and instability
Whether Gilheaney's proffered retraction evidence should be admitted
Application of Pringle and Benedetto to prison informer evidence
linked_authorities: R v Makanjuola (1995) 2 Cr App R(S) 469

confidence.notes: Detailed treatment of each ground and explicit dismissal; certification for House of Lords refused.

notes: Coutts murder appeal; Von Starck manslaughter alternative and internet evidence grounds largely rejected.

enrichment.short_title: R v Coutts: asphyxial sex manslaughter alternative and Jane Longhurst murder
key_facts: Graham Coutts was convicted of murdering Jane Longhurst by ligature strangulation during what he said was consensual asphyxial sex.
He stored and later burned her body; the prosecution case was deliberate killing to satisfy necrophiliac and strangulation fantasies supported by extensive internet pornography.
Both prosecution and defence agreed at trial that manslaughter should not be left to the jury as an alternative verdict.
He was sentenced to life imprisonment with a 30-year minimum term under Schedule 21 of the 2003 Act.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction and sentence by leave of the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeal dismissed on all grounds; sentence appeal partly allowed, reducing the minimum term to 26 years with ten months remand credit.
enrichment.ratio: A judge need not leave manslaughter where prosecution and defence agree it would be unfair and the only viable manslaughter basis rests on a wholly different factual scenario from the prosecution case; Von Starck does not require an alternative verdict that would transform the case the defendant had to meet.
legal_issues: Whether the judge was obliged to leave manslaughter despite defence and prosecution agreement
Admissibility of internet pornography evidence to rebut accident
Whether necrophilia allegations were supported by evidence
Transitional minimum term under Schedule 22 paragraph 10
linked_authorities: Von Starck v The Queen [2000] 1 WLR 1270

confidence.notes: Long judgment with clear disposals on each ground; Von Starck analysis is authoritative though fact-intensive.

notes: Gallaher pension GMP increases; rectification of 1987 deeds ordered after common intention analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Gallaher Ltd v Gallaher Pensions: GMP pension increases and rectification
key_facts: Gallaher Ltd sought to limit 2% limited price indexation under 1987 scheme amendments to pension increases above the Guaranteed Minimum Pension element.
Rule 7A introduced by the 1987 deeds was said to have been intended not to increase the GMP portion, but the wording covered all pensions in payment.
The 1989 deeds removed a ten-year cap on the increases; member representative defendants resisted the employer's interpretation and rectification claims.
The trustee took a neutral position while the employer also pursued Hastings Bass and Gibbon v Mitchell set-aside arguments.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery claim for declaration, rectification or setting aside of 1987 and 1989 pension scheme amendment deeds.
enrichment.outcome: Rectification of the 1987 deeds ordered in the terms sought; issues on the 1989 deeds did not arise; Hastings Bass and related claims failed or became unnecessary.
enrichment.ratio: Where employer and trustee objectively intended rule 7A increases to apply only to pension in payment above the GMP but the deeds were worded more broadly, rectification is available to give effect to that common intention; breach of fiduciary duty by the trustee would also have vitiated the deeds absent rectification.
legal_issues: Whether 'pensions in payment' in rule 7A excluded the GMP element
Availability of rectification for the 1987 deeds
Application of Re Hastings-Bass and Gibbon v Mitchell
Whether representative members were bona fide purchasers for value without notice
linked_authorities: Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896

confidence.notes: Final rectification order and detailed GMP background are clearly recorded; 1989 deed issues were not decided.

notes: Gatwick safeguarding blight JR; Sullivan J held written representations and planning inquiry were adequate review mechanisms.

enrichment.short_title: Persimmon Homes v SoS Transport: Gatwick runway safeguarding and CNES blight
key_facts: The 2003 Future of Air Transport White Paper safeguarded land for a wide-spaced second runway at Gatwick after 2019 as a fallback to Heathrow expansion.
Persimmon and a consortium sought to develop 2,700 homes at Crawley North East Sector (CNES), blighted by Article 14 directions linked to the policy.
The claimants accepted the policy was lawful but challenged the failure to institute continual proactive review after new noise contours and hybrid runway options emerged.
The Secretary of State maintained review could occur when circumstances required and that CNES arguments could be tested at a planning inquiry.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's refusal to establish a separate review mechanism for Gatwick wide-spaced runway safeguarding policy.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; Sullivan J held written representations to the Secretary of State and the statutory planning inquiry process were sufficient review mechanisms.
enrichment.ratio: Fairness does not require a non-statutory hearing or inquiry to review a lawfully adopted national aviation policy where consultees may make written representations and may deploy their case, including hybrid runway capacity arguments, at a planning inquiry on the blighted development.
legal_issues: Whether fairness required proactive government research into hybrid runway capacity
Whether written representations were an adequate review mechanism
Whether the Secretary of State was obliged to commission BAA or CAA studies to mitigate blight
Use of Halcrow rather than independent consultants to assess review need
linked_authorities: R (Medway Council) v Secretary of State for Transport [2003] JPL 583
Binney & Anscombe v Secretary of State for the Environment [1983] JPL 871

confidence.notes: Detailed reasoning on available review mechanisms though many technical planning disputes were expressly not for the court.

notes: Transitional Sex Offenders Act issue; invalid post-commencement restraining order quashed without substituting five-year SOPO.

enrichment.short_title: Monument: invalid restraining order after Sexual Offences Act 2003 commencement
key_facts: Andrew Monument was sentenced on 23 April 2004 to eight months' imprisonment for making indecent images of children and registered under section 2 of the 1997 Act for ten years.

On 14 May 2004, after the 2003 Act commenced, the Crown applied under the slip rule to add a three-year section 5A restraining order banning computer use; all parties overlooked the legislative change.
The trial judge later accepted the order was unlawful; the 1997 Act power no longer existed and a Sexual Offences Prevention Order required a minimum five-year term.
The defendant did not resist an order in principle but the judge had expressly limited any restraining order to three years.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Out-of-time appeal against the post-commencement restraining order, referred to the full Court of Appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the 14 May restraining order was invalid and quashed, and the court could not substitute a five-year Sexual Offences Prevention Order without dealing with the appellant more severely on appeal.
enrichment.ratio: A restraining order purportedly made under the repealed 1997 Act after commencement of the 2003 Act is invalid and cannot be saved by section 17(2) of the Interpretation Act; section 11(3) of the Criminal Appeal Act prevents substituting a mandatory five-year SOPO where the judge below would not have imposed that longer term.
legal_issues: Whether section 155 slip-rule variation could validate a post-repeal restraining order
Whether section 17(2) treated the order as a Sexual Offences Prevention Order
Whether the Court of Appeal could substitute a five-year SOPO under section 11(3)
Application of Beaney on serious harm from downloading indecent images

confidence.notes: Legislative transition issue and final quashing are clearly and fully reasoned.

notes: POCA civil recovery permission appeal; cocaine cash summary judgment and Article 6/7 arguments rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Assets Recovery Agency v Charrington: POCA civil recovery and cocaine cash
key_facts: Some £2.25 million in cash contaminated with cocaine was seized at Charrington's home after Felixstowe cocaine importation investigations implicating Curtis Warren and Mario Halley.
Charrington acted as a police informant but was not prosecuted; the Assets Recovery Agency later sought about £3.5 million held by Customs under POCA civil recovery.
He claimed the cash was commission from legitimate diamond dealing, supported by late statements later discounted by the court.
Collins J granted summary judgment; Charrington renewed an application for permission to appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal against a Part 24 summary judgment recovery order in favour of the Assets Recovery Agency.
enrichment.outcome: Permission application dismissed with costs; Laws LJ held Charrington's diamond-dealing account was incredible and civil recovery proceedings were not criminal for Article 6 or Article 7 purposes.
enrichment.ratio: Civil recovery under Part 5 of POCA is a civil not criminal process for Convention purposes, following Butler and Webb; long delay in bringing recovery proceedings does not disable the director where cash was lawfully retained pending proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether the cash was proceeds of unlawful conduct
Whether POCA recovery proceedings are criminal for Article 6 and Article 7
Whether delay and prior retention by Customs barred recovery
Weight of late police witness statements supporting the defendant

confidence.notes: Permission refusal and Convention classification are clearly reasoned though merits were not fully retried.

notes: Halston investment deceit trial; Simons held liable for falsified intra-group debt certificate.

enrichment.short_title: Halston v Simons: deceit over HGE intra-group indebtedness certificate
key_facts: Halston invested in Harvey Goldsmith Entertainments Ltd under a 1997 shareholders' agreement requiring certification that intra-group indebtedness did not exceed £2.8 million.
The finance director Ed Simons signed a certificate to that effect, but the true indebtedness was about £3.8 million.
Accounts staff said Simons altered a management spreadsheet to reduce shown inter-company debt from about £3.6 million to £2.6 million before completion.
HGE later collapsed after cashflow strain and losses on the Total Eclipse promotion; Halston lost its investment and loans apart from guarantee recoveries.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Queen's Bench trial of a deceit claim for damages arising from the share purchase and loan transaction.
enrichment.outcome: Simons held liable in deceit; Halston entitled to damages for its full loss subject to recoveries under Smith New Court and Doyle v Olby principles.
enrichment.ratio: A knowingly false certificate of intra-group indebtedness inducing investment gives rise to deceit liability for losses directly flowing from the transaction; where the misstatement left the company with an inadequate capital base unable to withstand later losses, the deceit caused the investment loss.
legal_issues: Whether Simons knowingly falsified the indebtedness certificate
Whether Halston relied on the certificate in completing the agreement
Causation and mitigation of investment losses
Measure of damages under Smith New Court and Doyle v Olby
linked_authorities: Smith New Court Securities Ltd v Citibank [1997] AC 254
Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896

confidence.notes: Detailed factual findings on spreadsheet alteration and clear deceit liability determination.
